lead: A Turing machine M accepts a string w when the run that starts with w on the tape ends in the accept state. The language L(M) is the set of all strings that pass this test. This definition turns a machine into a language recognizer: each input string gets one of three fates, accept, reject, or loop forever. The idea matters because it is the standard link between computation and formal languages, used in parsing, protocol checks, and in the theory of what software can and cannot decide.
prereq: You need: instantaneous descriptions and the yield relation from 5.1.

blocks.text: A run of M begins in the start state q<sub>0</sub> with input w written on the tape. Each move rewrites one cell, changes state, and moves the head left or right. Write α q β for the instantaneous description: α is the tape left of the head, q is the state, β is the tape from the head rightward. The symbol □ is the blank. The machine accepts w if some sequence of moves from q<sub>0</sub>w reaches a configuration whose state is q<sub>accept</sub>. The tape content at that moment does not matter.
L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* | q<sub>0</sub>w ⊢* α q<sub>accept</sub>β for some α, β }
blocks.where: L(M) is the language of M; Σ* is the set of all strings over input alphabet Σ; q<sub>0</sub>w is the starting configuration; ⊢* means zero or more moves; q<sub>accept</sub> is the accept state; α and β are the tape strings left and right of the head at acceptance.

blocks.text: Acceptance is reaching q<sub>accept</sub>, not merely stopping. If the machine halts in another state, it rejects. If no move is defined for the current state and cell, it halts and rejects under the usual convention. If it never reaches q<sub>accept</sub> and never halts, it loops. Then w is not in L(M), but M has not rejected w either; the run is unfinished.

sections.h3: Acceptor, decider, and the name of the language

blocks.text: A Turing machine used this way is an acceptor: it may loop on strings outside its language. A decider is stronger: it halts on every input, so every string is either accepted or rejected. Every decider is an acceptor, but an acceptor need not be a decider. The table shows the contrast.

blocks.text: The class of languages accepted by some Turing machine is called recursively enumerable (RE). Some syllabi call L(M) the language of the TM, or say M recognizes L(M). The class accepted by some decider is called recursive. The recursive versus recursively enumerable distinction is developed in Unit 6. Here, keep the operational meaning: L(M) contains exactly the strings on which M reaches q<sub>accept</sub>.

This is why acceptance is weaker than deciding. If you simulate M on w and the simulation has not stopped after a long time, you have no proof that w is outside L(M). The machine may still accept later. A decider gives a definite yes or no after finite time.
For a fixed machine and a fixed input, you test membership by simulating the run.

items: Write w on the tape, set the state to q<sub>0</sub>, and put the head on the first symbol of w.
Read the current cell symbol a and look up δ(q, a) for the current state q.
If δ(q, a) is undefined, halt and reject.
Apply the move: write the new symbol, change to the new state, and move the head one cell left or right.
If the new state is q<sub>accept</sub>, accept. If it is q<sub>reject</sub>, reject.
Otherwise repeat. If the run never reaches q<sub>accept</sub> or q<sub>reject</sub>, it loops; do not call that a reject.

blocks.text: The order matters in an exam answer. Show the starting configuration, show each rewrite, and stop at q<sub>accept</sub> or q<sub>reject</sub>. A run that ends in q<sub>reject</sub> is a rejected string. A run that has no next move is also a rejected string. A run that goes on forever gives no decision from the machine; the string is simply not in L(M).

spec.aria: Two tapes, 001 and 000, with the head positions 0, 1, 2 (and 3) marked below; 001 stops on its 1 in qaccept, 000 stops on the blank in qreject.

examples.question: A Turing machine M has moves δ(q<sub>0</sub>,0)=(q<sub>0</sub>,0,R), δ(q<sub>0</sub>,1)=(q<sub>accept</sub>,1,R), δ(q<sub>0</sub>,□)=(q<sub>reject</sub>,□,R). All other moves are undefined. Trace the runs on input 001 and input 000. State whether M accepts each string. Use accept = 1 and reject = 0 in the numerical answer.
steps: Start 001: configuration q<sub>0</sub>001. The head is on the first 0.
Move 1: δ(q<sub>0</sub>,0)=(q<sub>0</sub>,0,R). Configuration becomes 0q<sub>0</sub>01. The head is on the second 0.
Move 2: again δ(q<sub>0</sub>,0)=(q<sub>0</sub>,0,R). Configuration becomes 00q<sub>0</sub>1. The head is on 1.
Move 3: δ(q<sub>0</sub>,1)=(q<sub>accept</sub>,1,R). Configuration becomes 001q<sub>accept</sub>□. The state is q<sub>accept</sub>, so 001 is accepted. Numerical value: 1.
Move 1: 0q<sub>0</sub>00. Move 2: 00q<sub>0</sub>0. Move 3: 000q<sub>0</sub>□. The head is on the blank after the input.
Move 4: δ(q<sub>0</sub>,□)=(q<sub>reject</sub>,□,R). Configuration becomes 000□q<sub>reject</sub>□. The state is q<sub>reject</sub>, so 000 is rejected. Numerical value: 0.
examples.answer: M accepts 001 and rejects 000; the numerical outputs are 1 and 0.

traps: Acceptance is reaching q<sub>accept</sub>, not merely stopping. Halting in q<sub>reject</sub> or with no move is rejection.
A loop is not a rejection. If M loops on w, then w ∉ L(M), but M has not rejected w.
Do not confuse L(M) with the set of strings on which M halts. L(M) is only the accepted strings.
Undefined transition means halt and reject under the usual convention; some definitions use an explicit q<sub>reject</sub>. Read the definition given in the question.
The accept state must be reached. A machine that stops in a non-accepting state has not accepted, even if the tape looks correct.

quiz.q: Write the set notation for L(M) when acceptance is by final state.
quiz.a: L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* | q<sub>0</sub>w ⊢* α q<sub>accept</sub>β for some tape strings α and β }.

quiz.q: A machine halts on w in q<sub>reject</sub>. Is w accepted? Is w in L(M)?
quiz.a: No. Halting in q<sub>reject</sub> is rejection, so w is not accepted and w ∉ L(M).

quiz.q: State one difference between a Turing acceptor and a Turing decider.
quiz.a: A decider halts on every input. An acceptor may loop on some inputs outside its language.

quiz.q: Use M from the worked example. Trace input 01 and state the result.
quiz.a: q<sub>0</sub>01 → 0q<sub>0</sub>1 → 01q<sub>accept</sub>□. The machine accepts 01 in 2 moves.

quiz.q: Use M from the worked example. Trace input 10 and state the result.
quiz.a: q<sub>0</sub>10 → 1q<sub>accept</sub>0. The machine accepts 10 in 1 move.

quiz.q: Can a Turing machine accept a string without halting? Explain in one sentence.
quiz.a: No. Acceptance is reaching q<sub>accept</sub>, which is a halting accept configuration; a run that never halts never reaches it.

quiz.q: M accepts exactly the strings over {0,1} that contain at least one 1, and M loops on 000. What is L(M)? Has M rejected 000?
quiz.a: L(M) = { w ∈ {0,1}* | w contains at least one 1 }. 000 ∉ L(M), but M loops on 000, so it has not rejected 000.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same definition appears in modern software as a recognizer for a language of valid inputs, such as a parser that may loop on malformed input. Verification tools search for a run that reaches an error state, which is acceptance by a final state in reverse. Researchers study Turing-recognizable languages because they model semi-decision procedures: a yes can be found in finite time, but a no may not. Search for "Turing recognizable", "recursively enumerable language", and "decider versus acceptor" to go further.
